content: Methyl salicylate, with the chemical formula C6H4(HO)COOCH3, is also referred to as salicylic acid methyl ester, oil of wintergreen, betula oil, or methyl-2-hydroxybenzoate. It is a naturally occurring compound found in various plant species. Some of these plants are commonly known as wintergreens, which is the origin of one of its names. Plants that produce methyl salicylate synthesize this organic ester, which is a combination of an organic acid and an alcohol, likely as a defense mechanism against herbivores. Beyond its toxic properties, methyl salicylate may also serve as a signaling molecule, functioning as a pheromone to alert neighboring plants of potential threats, such as pathogens like the tobacco mosaic virus. When plants are infested with herbivorous insects, the release of methyl salicylate can attract beneficial predatory insects that help eliminate the herbivores. While many plants produce this compound in trace amounts, certain species produce it in detectable quantities, identifiable by their scent. These include most species in the family Pyrolaceae, particularly those in the genus Pyrola; some species in the genus Gaultheria of the family Ericaceae; and some species in the genus Betula of the family Betulaceae, especially those in the subgenus Betulenta. Methyl salicylate can be synthesized commercially by esterifying salicylic acid with methanol. Historically, it was distilled from the twigs of Sweet Birch (Betula lenta) and Eastern Teaberry (Gaultheria procumbens). Today, it is widely used to impart fragrance to various products and as an odor-masking agent for certain organophosphate pesticides. However, excessive application can lead to adverse effects, such as gastrointestinal and renal issues. Additionally, methyl salicylate is known to attract male orchid bees, which collect the compound to synthesize their own pheromones. This property makes it a useful bait for studying these bees. Methyl salicylate also has applications in microscopy and immunohistochemistry, as it can clear pigments from plant or animal tissue samples, making structures more visible under a microscope. This clearing process typically takes only a few minutes but requires prior dehydration of the tissue in alcohol. Furthermore, methyl salicylate can be used as a transfer agent to manually replicate images onto surfaces. In its pure form, methyl salicylate is toxic, particularly when ingested. The lowest reported lethal dose in adult humans is 101 mg/kg of body weight. It has been fatal to small children in doses as low as 4 mL. A notable case involved a 17-year-old cross-country runner from Notre Dame Academy on Staten Island, who died on April 3, 2007, after her body absorbed toxic levels of methyl salicylate due to excessive use of topical muscle-pain relief products.
